A1_Title.title: BCM2_09_SEG7257 [Segment Logic – Axioms of the Behavioral Change Segments]

A2_Scope.description: This chapter specifies the axiomatic and operational structure of segment logic in the Behavioral Change Model (BCM 2.0/BEATRIX). It defines segment-based heterogeneity, segment-specific willingness and awareness dynamics, transition rules, intervention sensitivity, and model couplings for all behavioral-economic applications, simulations, and intervention architectures.

goals: Precise, model-integrated representation of segmented behavioral dynamics in populations and organizations
Operationalization of heterogeneity along the Behavioral Change Journey, the willingness function, and all utility dimensions
Enablement of segment-specific interventions and their evaluation
Ensuring measurability, comparability, and auditability of segments and their transitions

A4_Axioms.name: Segment-Based Heterogeneity
A4_Axioms.definition: Populations are heterogeneous and consist of distinct behavioral segments.
A4_Axioms.formal: S ∈ {Leaders, EarlyAdopters, Pragmatists, Followers, Skeptics, Resistants}
A4_Axioms.notes: Segment labels are BCM-conform terms; segment set is the default taxonomy for BCM2_09.

A4_Axioms.name: Willingness Is Segment-Dependent
A4_Axioms.definition: Each segment has its own willingness function.
A4_Axioms.formal: W_S(t) = f(N_ind,S, N_kol,S, N_id,S, A_S(t), B_S(t), H_S(t))
A4_Axioms.notes: Weights, distortions, and sensitivities vary by segment.

A4_Axioms.name: Awareness Acts Differentially
A4_Axioms.definition: Awareness affects different segments with different intensity.
A4_Axioms.notes: Leaders and EarlyAdopters are typically more awareness-sensitive than Skeptics and Resistants.

A4_Axioms.name: Social Influence Is Asymmetrically Distributed
A4_Axioms.definition: Some segments (e.g., Leaders, EarlyAdopters) exert disproportionate influence on others.

A4_Axioms.name: Segment Transitions Are Probabilistic
A4_Axioms.definition: Individuals can move between segments with transition probabilities.

A4_Axioms.name: Collective Utility Acts Indirectly
A4_Axioms.definition: In segmented populations, collective utility takes effect via social norms and identity rather than directly.

A4_Axioms.name: Segmentation Is Decisive for Modeling and Intervention
A4_Axioms.definition: One-size-fits-all measures are inefficient and can generate resistance.
A4_Axioms.notes: Interventions must be planned segment-differentiated for effectiveness and to avoid backfire/resistance patterns.

requirements: Loaded modules for utility functions (BCM2_01_INU, BCM2_02_KNU, BCM2_03_IDN), awareness (BCM2_05_AWX), willingness (BCM2_06_KOM / BCM2_07_WTX)
Definition of the segmentation grid for the target population or organization
Context vector defined for each segment analysis

integration: Direct linkage with the willingness function, awareness, utility modules, and the Behavioral Change Journey (BCM2_10_JNY)
Segment logic functions as a filter and amplifier for all intervention and simulation architectures

constraints: Only BCM-conform terminology and segment labels are used
No application for individual diagnostics; exclusively for model-based change and intervention architecture
No use of psychological, suggestive, or system-external terms

A10_License_and_Usage.license: Use restricted to the BEATRIX/BCM 2.0 architecture with explicit initialization and inclusion of all mandatory modules.
conditions: All mandatory modules must be integrated
Commercial and scientific use requires written permission from FehrAdvice & Partners AG

summary: Enables precise, operationalizable modeling of societal change processes
Structures heterogeneity without unnecessary model complication
Allows targeted, empirically testable segment interventions
Fully compatible with willingness, the Behavioral Change Journey, and all meta-axioms

non_normative_extensions.name: Axiom of Imperfection (extended 2025)
non_normative_extensions.definition: In any population there exist residual segments (Always-Lie, Always-Truth) that act deterministically under certain contexts. These segments are not absolute constants: depending on identifiability, trust in institutions, and identity stability, they may transition into the Middle segment or flip into the opposite Always segment. The Middle segment remains the central dynamic space.
implications: Residual segments are stable attractors but not absolute constants.
Identifiability (R), institutional trust (UNS-INS), and identity (IDN) govern transitions.
The Middle segment is the key space (80–90%) and absorbs parts of L and T.
Radical breaks are modelable (e.g., T → L or M → T).
Simulations become more realistic because transition paths are explicit.
